newsitem.title: USA: Reno urges passage of victims' rights amendments.
newsitem.headline: Reno urges passage of victims' rights amendments.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno said Wednesday she and President Clinton believed a constitutional amendment was needed to balance the rights of crime victims and defendents.
"The president and I have concluded that an amendment to the Constitution to protect victims' rights is warranted," Reno said at Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.

"Unless the Constitution is amended to ensure basic rights to crime victims, we will never correct the existing imbalance in the country between defendents' irreducible constitutional rights and the current haphazard patchwork of victims' rights," she said.

Reno said a constitutional amendment would force courts to give greater consideration to victims' rights, which she said were often ignored, and encourage increased cooperation by victims and their families with law enforcement.

The proposed amendment would give crime victims the right to attend and participate in trials and parole hearings on their case and be notified about any proceedings or the release or parole of the person convicted for the crime.

Supporters say there are 15 specific rights in the Constitution for defendents including the right to a jury trial and an attorney, the right to confront witnesses and protection against self-incrimination but none for victims.

This was Reno's first appearence before Congress since she rejected on Monday a Republican request for an independent counsel to investigate campaign fund raising activity by Clinton and other administration officials.

Reno could have been grilled about her decision, but Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican, asked members to put off any questions about the independent counsel until she returns on April 30 to keep the focus on victims' rights.

The proposed amendment has been introduced in both the House and Senate with bipartisan support. It needs a two-thirds majority vote in each chamber to pass and be sent to the states for ratification.

There are victims' rights amendments in 29 states, but Reno said they were not as comprehensive as a constitutional amendment. She said crime victims could be given rights without jeopardising the rights of defendents.
But Sen. Edward Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat, said it would be better to protect victims' rights through a federal law, rather than a constitutional amendment.
"The Constitution is not a legal code on which we should legislate policy. It is not a bulletin board for attaching policy positions, no matter how appealing the positions are," Kennedy said.

The Constitution has been amended 27 times since it was written in 1789. Dozens of amendments have been introduced since Republicans took over Congress in 1995, including ones to require a balanced federal budget, limit congressional terms and ban flag-burning, but none has passed.
